title: Total War: Conducting World War I
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: When the soldiers of Europe marched off in August 1914, almost everyone believed they would be home by Christmas, expecting a short war. Instead the conflict ground on for over four years and reached nearly every corner of the globe, one of history's great miscalculations.

Industrial technology — machine guns, artillery, barbed wire, and railroads — made defense far more powerful than offense in World War I. Soldiers who charged across open ground were mowed down, so the only way to survive was to dig into the earth.

By the end of 1914 two continuous lines of trenches stretched about 450 miles across France and Belgium, from the English Channel to the Swiss border. Between them lay 'no man's land,' a churned wasteland of mud, craters, and barbed wire.

The machine gun could cut down hundreds of attacking soldiers a minute, while massed artillery churned the battlefield and killed more men than any other weapon in the war. Barbed wire entangled and exposed attackers.

At the Battle of the Somme in 1916, the British suffered about 57,000 casualties — roughly 19,000 of them dead — on the first day alone. The months-long battle produced over a million casualties on all sides and moved the front only a few miles.

At the Battle of Verdun in 1916, French and German forces together suffered an estimated 700,000 casualties over ten months of fighting, a symbol of the war's industrialized slaughter for minimal territorial gain.

New technologies meant to break the stalemate mostly added to the horror: poison gas (chlorine, then mustard gas) blinded and choked men, tanks were introduced by the British in 1916 but were slow and unreliable, and airplanes moved from scouting to bombing and dogfighting.

German U-boats waged submarine warfare on shipping. Germany's unrestricted submarine warfare, which sank neutral and passenger ships such as the Lusitania, helped draw the United States into the war in 1917, tipping the balance toward the Allies.

Total war is the mobilization of an entire society's population, economy, and resources for the war effort. In total war the line between soldier and civilian blurs, and the whole nation is directed toward victory, not just its army.

In WWI, governments took unprecedented control of their economies: directing factories to produce war materials, rationing food and goods, setting prices and wages, and managing labor to meet the war's staggering demands.
Many powers introduced or expanded military conscription (the draft) to fill the endless demand for soldiers, calling up millions of men across all the major combatant nations.

With millions of men at the front, women entered the industrial workforce in huge numbers, building shells in munitions factories and keeping economies running. This experience fed directly into the postwar expansion of women's voting rights in several countries.

States waged war on the home front through propaganda — posters, films, and a controlled press to sustain morale and demonize the enemy — and through censorship and new restrictions on civil liberties to suppress dissent.

Britain and France mobilized hundreds of thousands of colonial troops and laborers. Soldiers from India fought in Europe and the Middle East; troops from French West and North Africa and Senegal fought on the Western Front; and Vietnamese, Chinese, and African workers labored behind the lines.

Colonial subjects who served in WWI often returned home with a sharpened sense that the promises and ideals of their imperial rulers should apply to them too, helping fuel the nationalist and anti-colonial movements of the following decades.

WWI fighting was global: the Ottoman Empire fought campaigns across the Middle East (including Gallipoli and the Arab Revolt), German colonies in Africa and the Pacific were seized by the Allies, Japan took German holdings in China and the Pacific, and battles raged in East Africa.
Within the Ottoman Empire, WWI became the context for the Armenian Genocide, in which the Ottoman government deported and killed an estimated one million or more Armenians.

Self-determination, associated with U.S. President Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points, was the principle that peoples should choose their own government. It was applied in Europe but largely denied to colonized peoples, a contradiction that fueled anti-colonial nationalism.
World War I destroyed four empires: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and Ottoman. They were replaced by new states and redrawn borders, especially in Eastern Europe and the Middle East.
The strains of total war helped trigger the Russian Revolution of 1917, which pulled Russia out of the war and led to the creation of the Soviet Union, the world's first communist state.

The Treaty of Versailles (1919) forced Germany to accept sole 'war guilt,' pay enormous reparations, surrender territory and colonies, and drastically reduce its military. Many Germans saw it as a humiliating dictate, and that bitterness helped fuel the later rise of Hitler.

World War I was the great hinge of the modern period: it killed about 17 million people, destroyed four empires, sparked the Russian Revolution, redrew the Middle East into European mandates, and through denied self-determination awakened anti-colonial movements.
